analysis.one_liner: Caps fossil-fuel carbon emissions and pays every lawful US resident an equal dividend from the permit auctions.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and it died in the Senate Finance Committee when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require oil refineries and petroleum importers, coal mines and coal importers, and natural gas suppliers to buy permits for the carbon dioxide their fuels emit. The number of permits would shrink each year, cutting US carbon emissions 80% below 2005 levels by 2040. All money raised would be returned as equal quarterly payments to every person lawfully present in the US with a valid Social Security number, excluding nonresident aliens. The bill would also charge fees on imports of carbon-intensive goods like steel and cement from countries without matching climate rules, and pay similar rebates to US exporters, so US manufacturers would not lose out to pollution-heavy competitors.
analysis.who_benefits: Most American households. Every lawful resident with a Social Security number would receive an equal quarterly dividend paid out of the auction proceeds, with the payment excluded from taxable income. Because higher-income households consume far more fossil energy than lower-income households, an equal-per-person dividend means a large majority of households would receive more in dividends than they pay in higher fuel and electricity prices. Everyone also benefits from slower climate change, since the cap falls to 80% below 2005 emissions by 2040. US steel, cement, glass, and other carbon-intensive manufacturers would gain protection from foreign competitors that face no carbon costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Most US households, especially lower-income ones

how_it_helps.text: The Treasury would hold at least four public auctions per year of carbon permits to refineries, coal mines, coal importers, petroleum importers, and natural gas suppliers, and the total number of permits would decline on a fixed schedule to 80% below 2005 emissions by 2040 [S3].

All auction proceeds and penalties would go into a Healthy Climate Trust Fund and be paid out as equal quarterly 'Healthy Climate Dividend Payments' to every individual lawfully present in the US with a valid Social Security number, excluding nonresident aliens; the payments are excluded from taxable income [S3].

Because the same dividend goes to every person while wealthier households burn more fuel, the design returns more cash to lower- and middle-income households than they pay in fuel-cost increases; the bill's findings state that stabilizing the climate 'must be done in a way that supports vibrant economic growth and a thriving middle class' [S3].

A border adjustment would impose carbon-equivalency fees on imports of carbon-intensive goods like iron, steel, aluminum, cement, glass, paper, and chemicals from countries without equivalent climate measures, and pay offsetting amounts to US exporters of those goods, protecting US manufacturing jobs and competitiveness [S3].
Permits held by a single entity would be capped at auction and in total, with rules intended to 'prevent speculation, manipulation, or hoarding of permits' [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil refineries, petroleum importers, coal mines, coal importers, and natural gas suppliers and processors, which would pay for permits covering the carbon dioxide from every ton of fuel they sell into US markets, with rising costs as the cap tightens. Their customers would pay some of that cost through higher gasoline, heating, and electricity prices, though for most households the dividend more than covers it. The bill also carves out an exemption from EPA regulation for greenhouse gases 'directly attributable to the production of animals for food,' sparing the livestock industry.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil, coal, and natural gas producers

drawbacks.text: Fuel and energy prices would rise for everyone, and households that use more than average energy, such as large rural homes or long-distance commuters, could receive less in dividends than they pay in higher costs [S3].

Nonresident aliens and anyone lawfully present without a valid Social Security number would pay higher fuel prices but receive no dividend, so part of the public bears the cost without the offset [S3].
The bill permanently exempts gases 'directly attributable to the production of animals for food' from EPA regulation, leaving a major agricultural source of greenhouse gases untouched [S3].

The bill allows Treasury to auction additional permits from future years when prices rise more than 50%, softening the near-term emissions cut in exchange for price stability, and permits can be banked for future years [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is strong for ordinary households: a hard, declining cap on fossil carbon with all proceeds returned equally per person is one of the most progressive ways to price carbon, and border fees protect manufacturing jobs. The main real costs are higher energy prices for high-energy-use households and for nonresident aliens who get no dividend, and a politically motivated exemption for livestock emissions. On balance the benefits to most working families and to climate stability outweigh those costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced by one senator with no cosponsors, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Van Hollen introduced S. 940 on March 28, 2019, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S5].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor; the Congress.gov cosponsors page shows 0 [S4].

The bill never advanced beyond its referral to Finance. The full action history lists only the introduction and the referral, with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action, and the Congress ended January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, coal, and natural gas producers, which kept selling carbon-heavy fuels without paying for their emissions, and are better off because the bill never moved. Everyone else got no climate law and no dividend, and the 2019 emissions cap that would have started the decline never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers that never paid for emissions

for.name: Sen. Chris Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Healthy Climate and Family Security Act of 2019 and shepherded its referral to the Finance Committee; no other senator joined him.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up; no hearing, no markup, no vote was ever scheduled during the entire two-year Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never allowed the bill to reach the floor at any point in the 116th Congress.

against.name: Fossil fuel industry
against.role: Oil, coal, and natural gas producers
against.what_they_did: Would have paid for every ton of carbon from fuels they sell; the bill died without ever reaching a vote, so they bore no cost.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no senator cosponsored the bill, so the partisan shape was never tested; the bill died with its single Democratic sponsor in a Republican-run committee.

industries.note: They would have had to buy permits for the carbon emitted by every barrel of crude and gallon of fuel sold in the US, with costs rising as the cap fell. Their interest in stopping the bill ran against the public's interest in both the dividend and the emissions cap.
Coal is the most carbon-intensive covered fuel, so mines and importers would have faced the steepest relative cost as the cap declined 80% below 2005 levels by 2040.
They would have purchased permits covering the carbon dioxide from the gas they deliver to end users, adding cost that their interest was to avoid.

industries.industry: Carbon-intensive manufacturers (steel, cement, aluminum, glass, paper, chemicals)
industries.note: Border fees would have been imposed on competing imports from countries without carbon rules and rebates paid to US exporters, protecting US factory jobs from pollution-based price competition.
The bill permanently exempts gases attributable to producing animals for food from the EPA regulatory mandate, leaving that major emissions source to no one's cost.
